title: An honest text backtest
objectives: Design a text-signal backtest that survives a cut-off check and the number of models tried.

screens.title: The best of twelve prompts
screens.prose: A researcher scores news with a language model, trying 12 prompt wordings over the 2 years after the model's cut-off, and reports the best: a Sharpe ratio of 2.1. `validation` level 3's haircut subtracts a generous allowance for what the best of $N$ noise strategies reaches over $T$ years, the rule of thumb $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$ (their best averages a little less).
screens.question: What is the haircut Sharpe ratio? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Divide by $\sqrt 2$, then subtract from 2.1.

byKey.noise: 1.58 is the allowance for the best of 12 noise strategies. Subtract it from 2.1.

explain.text: Twelve tries over two years give an allowance of about 1.58 (their best averages nearer 1.15), so the reported 2.1 is worth about 0.52 after the haircut.

screens.title: How many tries until 2 is noise?
screens.prose: Slide $T$, the years of clean data. The curve is the haircut allowance, a generous bound on the best Sharpe ratio that $N$ noise strategies reach.
screens.question: With $T = 2$ years, what is the smallest $N$ whose allowance is at least 2?

hints.text: Solve $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt 2 = 2$.
That is $\ln N = 4$, so $N = e^4$.
$e^4 = 54.6$; round up.

feedback.correct: $e^4 = 54.6$, so 55 tries: with two years of data, the allowance for the best of 55 noise strategies reaches 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Solve for $N$ and round up.

byKey.e4: 54.6 tries cannot happen; round up to a whole number.

explain.text: $\sqrt{2\ln N} = 2\sqrt 2$ gives $\ln N = 4$ and $N = e^4 \approx 54.6$, so 55. A desk that tries 55 prompts on two years should allow for a Sharpe near 2 from noise alone.

screens.title: Walk-forward folds
screens.prose: Fitting anything, even a threshold, on the whole clean window uses its future. **Walk-forward** validation (`validation` level 2) cuts the 500 clean days into 5 consecutive folds; each fold is traded with a threshold fitted on the folds before it, so the first fold only trains.
screens.question: How many days of out-of-sample P&L does this give?

hints.text: Each fold is 100 days.
Folds 2 to 5 are traded.

feedback.correct: Four folds of 100: 400 days, each traded with a threshold from earlier days only.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The first fold has no earlier data to fit on.

byKey.all: The first fold has nothing before it to fit on, so it only trains.
byKey.one: 100 is one fold. Folds 2 to 5 are all traded.

explain.text: Folds 2 to 5 give 400 out-of-sample days. Here the threshold is the mean score of the earlier folds; a vocabulary or a scaler would be fitted the same way.

screens.title: Costs
screens.prose: In the clean window the daily P&L has mean 0.0605% and standard deviation 0.9640%. Trading the sign each day turns the book over often; assume costs of 0.02% a day.
screens.question: What is the annualised Sharpe ratio after costs? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Subtract the cost from the daily mean first.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the cost off the mean, then annualise.

explain.text: Costs take the clean Sharpe from 1.00 to 0.67, a third of it gone. A text signal that trades daily must clear its costs as well as its leaks.

screens.title: Four designs, one signal
screens.prose: Four backtests of the same seeded scores. Only one design avoids every leak met in this level.
screens.question: Which Sharpe ratio should be reported?

Its threshold uses the whole window, future days included. It happens to be lower here: a leak can lower a result as well as raise it, and either way the figure is not a test.

feedback.correct: 0.47: the only figure every decision could have produced at the time.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each design for memory, timing and fitting leaks.

screens.title: Six months is not enough
screens.prose: A model's cut-off leaves only six months of clean data. A noise strategy's Sharpe ratio measured over $T$ years has a standard error of about $1/\sqrt T$ (`testing` level 3).
screens.question: What Sharpe ratio must six months show to be 1.96 standard errors above zero? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Solve $\text{SR}\sqrt T = 1.96$ with $T = 0.5$.

feedback.correct: $1.96/\sqrt{0.5} = 2.77$: below that, six months cannot tell skill from luck.

byKey.times: You multiplied by $\sqrt{0.5}$. A shorter window needs a higher Sharpe.
byKey.half: You divided by 0.5; divide by its square root.

explain.text: Six months needs a Sharpe above 2.77 before it is clear of noise at the usual level. Most real signals run between 0.5 and 2, so a short clean window rarely proves anything.

screens.title: One model, twelve prompts
screens.prose: A team reports a news signal's Sharpe ratio of 1.9 over 2 clean years. 'We used one model,' they say, 'so there is no multiple testing.' Their log shows 12 prompt wordings were tried.
screens.question: What is the haircut Sharpe ratio for 12 trials? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Each prompt wording is a trial.

feedback.correct: $1.9 - 1.5764 = 0.32$: most of the result is the selection.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count every prompt wording as a trial.

byKey.one: You took 'one model' as one trial. Each of the 12 prompts produced its own signal, and the best was kept.

explain.text: A prompt, a scoring scheme or a model version that produced a backtest is a trial. With 12 of them the 1.9 is worth about 0.32.

screens.title: The honest checklist
screens.prose: Put the steps of an honest text backtest in the order they are applied.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

Stamp every document with its first publication time
Join scores to decisions with a backward as-of join
Fit vocabularies, thresholds and scalers inside each walk-forward fold
Subtract trading costs from the out-of-sample P&L
Haircut the Sharpe ratio for every prompt and model tried

The haircut comes last, on the final out-of-sample figure.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each step needs the one before it.

screens.title: An honest text backtest
screens.prose:
What you assembled: a clean window after the cut-off, as-of stamps, past-only fitting in walk-forward folds, costs, and a haircut for $N$ trials over $T$ clean years,

$$\text{SR}_{\text{honest}} = \text{SR}_{\text{best}} - \frac{\sqrt{2\ln N}}{\sqrt T}.$$

options.why: The full sample includes memorised years.

options.text: The in-sample fit, since it uses the most data
options.why: In-sample figures are fitted to the answer.

hints.text: Which figure could a reader reproduce honestly?

feedback.correct: The out-of-sample figure, net of costs, haircut, with the window's length.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which figure has every leak removed?

widget.solution:
import bisect
import math


def honest_backtest(panel, docs, cutoff, folds, decision_time='16:30'):
    docs = sorted(docs, key=lambda d: d['published'])
    times = [d['published'] for d in docs]
    days = [(d, r) for d, r in zip(panel['dates'], panel['ret']) if d > cutoff]
    feat = []
    for d, r in days:
        i = bisect.bisect_right(times, d + ' ' + decision_time)
        feat.append(docs[i - 1]['score'] if i > 0 else None)
    n = len(days)
    b = [round(i * n / folds) for i in range(folds + 1)]
    pnl = []
    for k in range(1, folds):
        past = [f for f in feat[:b[k]] if f is not None]
        mu = sum(past) / len(past)
        for t in range(b[k], b[k + 1]):
            f = feat[t]
            pos = 0 if f is None else (1 if f > mu else -1 if f < mu else 0)
            pnl.append(pos * days[t][1])
    m = sum(pnl) / len(pnl)
    sd = math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in pnl) / (len(pnl) - 1))
    return m / sd * math.sqrt(252)

screens.title: The desk's review form
screens.prose: A portfolio manager asks you to draft the one question the desk's review form must ask of every model-scored signal before any capital is risked.
screens.question: Which question covers the most ground?

options.text: Is it out-of-sample after the cut-off, net, and haircut for all tries?
What was the best Sharpe ratio found in testing?
options.why: The best of many is the figure most inflated by selection.

options.text: Which language model produced the scores?
options.why: Useful, but a famous model leaks as easily as an obscure one.

options.text: Does the backtest cover at least ten full years?
options.why: Ten years before a recent cut-off is mostly memory; length is not cleanliness.

hints.text: Which question forces every check in this level?

feedback.correct: Out-of-sample after the cut-off, net of costs, haircut for the trials.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which question rules out memory, leaks, costs and selection together?

explain.text: That one question forces the clean window, as-of stamps, past-only fitting, costs and the haircut. A signal that cannot answer it is not ready for capital.

ideas: An honest text backtest uses the clean window after the cut-off, as-of stamps, and vocabularies, thresholds and scalers fitted inside walk-forward folds.
Costs come off the out-of-sample P&L, and every prompt, scoring scheme or model tried is a trial for the haircut $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$.
A short clean window cannot separate skill from luck: six months needs a Sharpe ratio near 2.8 to clear 1.96 standard errors.
